items.title: Savage Garden’s Darren Hayes’ Career Celebrated at Music In The House Gala
items.summary: The Australian singer and songwriter received two awards on the night.
items.body: It was anything but an ordinary Tuesday night (Aug. 27) in Sydney as Darren Hayes was feted with the Excellence in Community Award at the 17th annual Music In The House event. The ex- Savage Garden singer and songwriter was on hand at the Support Act fundraiser, presented at The Linseed House, The Grounds of Alexandria, where he doubled up with induction into APRA AMCOS’s Billions Club, in recognition of the pop group’s Billboard Hot 100 leader from 1997, “Truly Madly Deeply,” one of their two U.S. No. 1s. Savage Garden, the pairing of Hayes and Daniel Jones, was one of Australia’s biggest exports of the 1990s. Their self-titled debut album — which houses “Truly Madly Deeply” and top 10 hit “I Want You” — peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard 200, while sophomore and final release Affirmation , which houses No. 1 smash “I Knew I Loved You,” reached No. 6. The group split up in 2001. For the past quarter century, Hayes has enjoyed a solo career, one that has yielded five studio albums, most recently the 2022 release Homosexual . items.title: Life360 adds new pet care tools to help keep your household in sync
items.summary: The shared care logs might stop your dog scoring a second dinner.
items.body: Credit: Life360 TL;DR Life360 is rolling out new pet-related features, including shared care logs that help families track routines such as feedings. The update also brings some lighter extras, including Weekly Roundups and Zoomies Alerts. A new $7.99 Pet Tag lets someone who finds a lost pet contact its owner or share its location more easily. It’s apparently International Dog Day tomorrow, but you can be forgiven for forgetting — the timing lands right as many households are descending back into school-run chaos. This can make it a little tougher to keep track of who fed and walked your four-legged friend , but Life360 is keen to simplify things with some new shared pet-care features. As detailed in the press release , the new Care and Connection tools are rolling out now, with Shared Care logs doing a lot of the heavy lifting. Families can set recurring routines for walks, feedings, medications, litter cleaning, and more, while completed tasks are visible to everyone in the care circle. That should make it easier to see who has actually done what, and perhaps stop your dog from successfully convincing a second family member that dinner never happened.

items.title: Apps may keep giving us tools to break our addiction to them, but teens aren’t using them
items.summary: Guess how many teens use anti-doomscrolling features. Hint: It's NOT "practically everyone."
items.body: TL;DR Tools like Digital Wellbeing or Instagram’s Take a Break are built to interrupt addictive use cycles. In an ongoing Meta trial, a former data scientist shares just how few teens actually took advantage of the company’s tools. With teen accounts, Take a Break is now on by default, hopefully pushing numbers up a little. Are smartphones our best friends, or our worst enemies? Sometimes it feels like half the work companies are putting into new features are attempts to fix our addiction to others, like with the new Pause Point on Pixel 11 devices — or really anything Digital Wellbeing , for that matter. And while we seem to keep getting more and more new tools meant to save us from ourselves, are the most vulnerable people even using them? According to Meta, maybe not so much. Meta’s currently being sued by 29 states over claims of safety and privacy issues impacting its youngest users, and Bloomberg is sharing some of the details just revealed by a former Meta data scientist’s testimony.

items.summary: Our readers told us what the Pixel 12's focus should be, and it's not more AI.
items.body: Like it or not, Google has made AI a huge part of the Pixel experience, and that’s only become more obvious with the Pixel 11 series. Gemini Intelligence and other smart features were a major focus of this year’s launch — so much so that you’d assume this was what all the fans were screaming out for. It’s always quite tricky to know how true that is, so we were curious about where you think Google needs to go next with the Pixel 12. We recently asked our readers exactly that. My colleague Robert Trigg certainly has his own ideas about this direction, and made them abundantly clear in a recent article . His argument in a nutshell is that the Pixel 11 shows Google is approaching something of a hardware breaking point. He wasn’t unhappy with Google’s AI work, but pointed out that rival flagships are pushing ahead in fundamental areas such as battery capacity, charging speeds, camera hardware, and raw performance, while Pixels haven’t kept pace. With the Pixel 12 next to face that challenge, we asked you via a poll in the article whether Google should prioritize better hardware, even smarter AI, both, or simply more competitive prices.

items.body: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR Claude chat and Cowork now share the same memory. Claude will now add topics to memory as you chat, instead of summarizing conversations after they end. You’ll be able to turn “include sensitive topics in memory” on or off. It has been about a week since Anthropic gave Claude the ability to send emails in Gmail and manage files in Google Drive. Now the AI company is rolling out another feature. This feature will make switching back and forth between Claude chat and Cowork a little easier. Anthropic has announced that Claude Cowork now has memory, so you can spend less time re-explaining. Not only does Cowork have memory, but it also shares the same memory as chat. That means when you run a task in Cowork, Claude will remember it in chat, and vice versa.

items.title: Google Home automations not working right lately? Blame your TV
items.summary: Google Home automations aren't playing nicely with your TV, but Google is on the case.
items.body: TL;DR Google Home users are reporting automations tied to TV starters failing to run. Google confirms an investigation is underway into problems with TV-based automations. So far the reports we’ve seen involve TCL models, but it’s not clear if other brands are similarly impacted. If you’re looking to configure a really impressive smart home, Google Home automations are your best friend. While routines are great for pulling off complicated multi-device workflows, automations take that to the next level by, well, automating them — instead of manually activating a routine, automations begin all by themselves when their starter event occurs. At least, that’s the way things are supposed to work, but right now there’s a frustrating glitch impacting automations tied to TVs. Over on Reddit’s Google Home sub, users have been complaining about automations involving their TVs that fail to work . While you should be able to use events like powering your TV on or off to trigger an automation, Google Home just doesn’t seem to recognize when these starter events happen.

items.summary: Garmin launches the fēnix 9 and fēnix 9 Pro.
items.body: Credit: Garmin TL;DR The Garmin fēnix 9 has 50% more RAM and offers several new features. The fēnix 9 Pro features a new titanium case, offers 3,000 nits of brightness, and comes with a new green light mode. The base model starts at $999.99, while the Pro variant starts at $1,099.99. When Google launched the Pixel Watch 5 earlier this month, the company made the bold claim that its GPS route tracking accuracy surpassed the fēnix 8 Pro. While that is an impressive feat, what about the latest model from Garmin’s adventure smartwatches? Garmin expanded its portfolio today with the launch of the fēnix 9 and fēnix 9 Pro. In case you missed it, Garmin held an announcement event this morning where it unveiled the next entries in the fēnix line. The new multisport GPS smartwatches both come in three sizes: 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm. You’ll also be able to outfit them with the new ComfortFit accessory bands, which feature a split-weave design.

items.title: Nanoleaf panels might soon work with the Philips Hue app
items.summary: One less smart lighting app to fuss with.
items.body: TL;DR Newly leaked images show that Philips Hue could soon release an adapter to integrate Nanoleaf Shapes lights. This info comes after an icon depicting hexagonal wall lights was found in the Hue app. The adapter will purportedly cost about €40 in Europe and may go on sale in September. Back in June, a Philips Hue user spotted that the app had added a new light type icon for hexagonal panel lights that looks more than a little like lights offered by Nanoleaf. At the time, we assumed that meant that Hue was cooking up its own hexagonal panel lights — but now, it looks like the icon may actually have been Nanoleaf lights, after all. Smartlights.de has shared some information about an unannounced “wall light module” from Philips Hue. The report says that Hue will release a kind of adapter for Nanoleaf’s Shapes lights that’ll let users integrate the third-party wall lights into existing Hue setups.

items.body: المصري الشاب يستعد لكتابة التاريخ مع البلوجرانا تلقى المصري الشاب حمزة عبد الكريم مهاجم برشلونة نبأ سارًا، بعد أدائه اللافت للنظر في الفترة الإعدادية قبل انطلاق الموسم. وتألق حمزة عبد الكريم مع برشلونة خلال فترة الإعداد، وسجّل 4 أهداف في المباريات الودية التي شارك بها مع الفريق الكتالوني هذا الصيف. وبفضل أدائه في المباريات الودية، قرر الألماني هانز فليك مدرب برشلونة، قيد حمزة عبد الكريم مع الفريق الأول، في الموسم الحالي. وظهر على الموقع الرسمي لرابطة الدوري الإسباني "لا ليجا" ، بطاقة حمزة عبد الكريم رسميًا، حيث يحمل القميص رقم 29. ولعب عبد الكريم بعد انضمامه من الأهلي المصري، في يناير/كانون الثاني الماضي، مع فرق الشباب بالبلوجرانا، قبل أن ينضم إلى الفريق الأول بعد 6 أشهر فقط. وجلس النجم المصري الشاب صاحب الـ18 عامًا، على مقاعد بدلاء برشلونة في مباراته الأولى بالليجا يوم الأحد الماضي، التي انتهت بفوز كاسح للبارسا أمام إلتشي (5-0). يشار إلى أن حمزة عبد الكريم كان ضمن كتيبة منتخب مصر التي شاركت في كأس العالم 2026، حيث وصل الفراعنة إلى دور الـ16، قبل الخروج أمام الأرجنتين. يمكنكم مناقشة الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة

items.title: 5 reasons I may not go back to Spotify after trying YouTube Music

items.body: As is the case with millions of users around the world, I’ve been a loyal Spotify subscriber for as long as I can remember. The app works well across Android and iOS, there’s a great selection of music, and features like Jam and Spotify Connect have made my listening experience much more seamless across audio devices at home. I was happy to pay for the Premium Duo plan — until it was sneakily taken away. Spotify removed the Duo plan in India around November 2025, but as I had subscribed to it long before, I was able to continue with it, as it should be. Then came the email, one July morning this year, saying my Premium Duo plan was canceled due to an “issue” with my payment method. Nothing had changed, so it didn’t make any sense. I figured it was Spotify forcing me to upgrade to a higher-priced plan, and as it turned out, I wasn’t the only one who got the boot. Frustrated with this move, I decided to try other options.

As a day-one Pixel user ever since the first phone launched, I’ve usually been immune to all the troubles that tend to plague Google’s flagship. Well, as the saying goes, luck eventually does run out. I’ve had my Pixel 11 Pro for just five days, and it’s already a brick. A couple of days into my time with the Pixel 11 Pro (in the gorgeous Canyon colorway), I decided to do a factory reset and a fresh setup instead of copying over all my data from my previous phone, and here we are.

items.title: Google Home made users say the weirdest thing to set an alarm, but that’s over now
items.summary: It's a small fix, but a welcome one for anyone who relies on voice alarms daily.
items.body: TL;DR Some Google Home devices stopped setting alarms via voice command for several days. The bug hit both Google Assistant and Gemini for Home, affecting Nest speakers, displays, and even third-party devices like Lenovo smart displays. Google has confirmed the fix, and our own testing shows alarms are setting and triggering correctly again. Google Home has had a busy August, with Google rolling out several updates that make Gemini for Home smarter and add new capabilities to its smart home platform. But amid all those improvements, something as basic as setting an alarm suddenly stopped working for some users. Thankfully, Google has now confirmed that the issue affecting Nest and other Gemini-powered smart home devices has been fixed. For several days, users on Reddit reported that commands such as “Hey Google, set an alarm for 8:30 AM” would simply be ignored. Some found that alarms worked when set for an exact hour, while others had to ask Google to set an alarm first and then provide the time when prompted. One odd workaround involved saying “Hey Google, hi” before giving the alarm command.

items.title: The Pixel 11 Pro’s camera flash is a ‘LoLight’ thanks to HiLight
items.summary: Users complain that the Pixel 11 Pro's camera flash is a big downgrade over other phones, and HiLight could be to blame here.
items.body: Credit: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority TL;DR Reddit users report that the Google Pixel 11 Pro’s camera flash is significantly weaker than that of older Pixels and competitors. Our preliminary testing here at Android Authority shows the Pixel 11 Pro XL torch mode registered 89 lux compared to 123 lux on the Pixel 10 Pro XL. The physical diffuser added to the camera visor for the new HiLight LED array is likely the cause of the softer beam. Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro series introduces HiLight , a small array of ambient LEDs around the camera flash that give you some bits of information without requiring you to turn over or unlock your phone. Google ended up severely limiting HiLight’s functionality, and users had to resort to apps like HiLight Studio to unlock the LED’s full potential. As it turns out, Google gimped HiLight in more ways than one, with the LED flash itself also downgraded compared to the Pixel 10 series. Reddit user pcman2000 voiced their frustration with the Pixel 11 Pro’s camera flash, calling it “really weak” and the weakest among all the phones they tested, ranking it below the Pixel 9 Pro and even the iPhone 17e.

items.title: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a camera problem, and it has nothing to do with photo quality

items.body: I’ve spent years trying the latest book-style foldables, but none earned a permanent spot in my pocket once I finished testing them. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 7 came the closest with a thin-and-light design and truly flagship specs. Unfortunately, it suffered from the same problems as every other folding phone with a squarish inner screen aspect ratio. The form factor isn’t conducive to widescreen video content, as you’ll see large black bars at the top and bottom of the folding screen. Samsung built the wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 to specifically address this pain point, and it quickly won me over. Then, something happened that I didn’t expect. I found myself using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 unfolded in portrait orientation more than landscape.

It can diagnose battery and Wi-Fi issues, open specific settings, change things like brightness and dark mode, and explain Pixel features without making you hunt through Settings. It’s still a Labs feature and can get things wrong. Our testing produced inconsistent instructions for Magic Capture, so it isn’t completely reliable yet. A few days ago, we spotted Google testing a clever new Gemini trick that could save Pixel users from digging through the Settings app every time something goes wrong. That feature, called Device Help, is now appearing directly inside the Gemini app on some of our Pixel 11 series devices. First spotted by 9to5Google , Device Help is currently showing up on Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro models we’ve checked, including our Pixel 11 Pro XL units. It still has a “Labs” badge attached, though, which is Google’s way of telling you things may not always work as expected. And after putting it through a few tests, that’s exactly what we found.

items.body: The Pixel 11 series has left Google with something of a dilemma. Based on our time with the phones so far, they remain among the most enjoyable Android handsets to use, thanks largely to Google’s software experience and a growing collection of genuinely useful features. But our testing of the Tensor G6 shows that Google’s custom silicon is falling further behind rival flagship chips; early gaming tests suggest a familiar litany of issues; and a week with the Pixel 11 Pro suggests that many of Google’s newest AI tricks aren’t yet strong enough to make up the difference. items.title: Forget iPhones — this hack brings Quick Share to Kindles
items.summary: An unofficial project called Kindshare adds Quick Share to jailbroken Kindles, with a few key limitations.
items.body: Credit: Kaitlyn Cimino / Android Authority TL;DR An unofficial project brings Quick Share receiving to jailbroken Kindle devices. Kindshare lets you send files wirelessly from an Android phone, but the Kindle can’t send files back. The process is fairly technical, and compatibility may depend on your Kindle model and firmware version. Quick Share made an unexpected leap beyond Android last year when Google made it compatible with Apple’s AirDrop . Now it’s more or less reached another device you probably wouldn’t have expected, as an unofficial project lets you send files from an Android phone straight to a jailbroken Kindle. As spotted by Hackaday , developer unrealJune has created Kindshare, an open-source project that adds Quick Share receiving to compatible Kindles. Once everything is set up, the Kindle can appear as a destination in Quick Share, letting you send files over wirelessly.

The app is displaying an error message that reads “Spotify isn’t responding.” It’s unclear what the cause of the problem is. Sometimes being an Android Auto user can feel like playing a game of whack-a-mole. A bug appears, a fix is rolled out, and another bug appears shortly after. For example, a fix for a glitch that caused connections to drop or freeze was recently released . Now, a new bug has shown up, and it’s preventing users from streaming their music and podcasts. items.title: The Pixel 11 Pro XL is built to last and easy to fix, teardown finds
items.summary: It's pricey, but at least you'll be able to hold onto it a few years.
items.body: TL;DR JerryRigEverything’s Zack Nelson has tested the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s durability and repairability. The phone didn’t bend in Nelson’s durability test, and key components are relatively simple to swap out. Nelson calls the Pixel 11 Pro XL “one of the easiest phones to repair of 2026.” It looks like it should be relatively easy to make the Pixel 11 Pro last. The XL version has now undergone the JerryRigEverything treatment, and the phone held up nicely to Zack Nelson’s usual battery of abuse. The teardown video also shows that common repairs should be relatively simple, with both the display and the battery removable with just a few minutes of work. The video shows that the 11 Pro XL barely bends or flexes at all as Nelson wrenches on it, so the phone should hold up fine in case you sit down with it in your back pocket. Despite Google’s claim that the 11 Pro’s display is “more than twice as scratch-resistant than previous models” thanks to a new coating, though, it still scratches at level six with deeper grooves at a level seven.

Now Playing remains one of the most compelling reasons to buy a Pixel still . In March this year, Google brought a major update to Now Playing, advancing it with its own dedicated app . items.body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority A few years ago, Chrome introduced Manifest V3 and began phasing out the older Manifest V2 technology used by some of the most advanced browser extensions. items.title: Nintendo just went nuclear on Switch emulators (again)
items.summary: Nintendo just can't stand Switch games running on anything other than a Switch.
items.body: TL;DR Nintendo has filed seven new DMCA notices taking down over 400 GitHub repositories related to Switch emulators. The notice took down repos for emulators such as Suyu, Skyline, and several others. It’s no secret that Nintendo has historically taken an extremely strict stance against emulators and people using its IP without permission. A few months ago, the company sent DMCA notices to take down several Switch emulators whose code was hosted on GitHub. Now, the company has thrown another proverbial Donkey Kong barrel at more such GitHub repositories. Nintendo has filed seven DMCA complaints with GitHub to take down over 400 repositories related to Switch emulators in a single day (via TorrentFreak ). This includes emulators like Suyu, which gained popularity after the Yuzu emulator shut down in 2024. According to the DMCA notice displayed publicly on the Suyu repository, GitHub took down all 311 repositories in the network due to Nintendo’s DMCA notice.

There are plenty of Google apps you probably use every day, but Android Pulse is definitely not one of them. In fact, you may not even know it exists.
